title: Google Docs for translators on Mac: translate, check terms and review files
metaTitle: Google Docs for Translators on Mac: Translate and Review

intro: You can use Google Docs for translation work on a Mac in your browser, with three built-in tools. Use Tools > Translate document for a first pass, Edit > Find and replace for term checks, and offline editing in Chrome for work away from a connection. This page covers each tool, its limits, and the mistakes that cause trouble later. It also shows where Lazur helps while you work.
tldr: Use Tools > Translate document for a first pass. The translated copy opens in a new window and is also saved to Google Drive.
Check comments, footnotes, headers and footers by hand. The official translate page does not say which parts get translated.
Use Edit > Find and replace for term checks, and test first whether it reaches comments and footnotes.
Offline editing needs Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge plus the Google Docs Offline extension. Private browsing does not work.
Lazur guides you, points at things, answers out loud and types drafts. It does not click buttons or edit files for you.

blocks.text: Most translators on a Mac work in a browser tab. Google's help pages describe Google Docs in a browser and do not describe a separate Mac app. This guide assumes Chrome or another browser on your Mac. Google does not date its help pages, so check the menus on your own screen before you follow a path word for word.
How to translate a whole document in Google Docs on Mac
Use the built-in translation for a first pass. It creates a new translated copy, so your original file stays as it was. Open the document in your browser first, then follow these steps.

items: Open the document in Google Docs in Chrome or another browser on your Mac.
Click Tools in the menu bar, then choose Translate document.
Enter a name for the new file.
Pick the language you want from the list.
Click Translate. The translated copy opens in a new window and is also saved in Google Drive.

blocks.text: The menu path is Tools > Translate document. Google's help page gives these steps for a computer. On a Mac, the command lives in the menu bar at the top of the screen, so use the menu rather than a right-click.
Why is Translate document missing in Google Docs?

This is the snag the official help page warns about. It says that if Translate document is missing, the file is likely in Microsoft Office editing mode. You must convert it to Google Docs first. Then run the command on the converted copy.

blocks.title: Convert first
blocks.text: Convert the Word or other Office file to Google Docs before you translate. Then run Tools > Translate document on the converted copy, not on the original Office file.

Here is a common case. A client sends a Word file with a glossary. You open it in Drive, the Tools menu has no translate command, and the file is in Office mode. Convert it, then translate. Keep the Word original untouched in case the client asks for it.
What the built-in translation does not cover

The official translate page does not state document length or file-type limits. It also does not say which parts of a document get translated. Comments, footnotes, headers and footers are not named. Treat the output as a first draft, and check those parts by hand.

items: Read the whole translated copy from top to bottom, not just the first page.
Open each footnote and check that its text was translated.
Check headers and footers on every page, since the help page does not name them.
Read every comment and check that its meaning still makes sense.
Look at tables and lists. Check that they still line up with the source.

blocks.text: Check names, numbers and dates on their own. A first-pass translation can keep the wrong format or miss a unit. Read each one against the source before you send the file.
Check terms with Find and replace on Mac
Glossary checks are where Google Docs helps most. Open Edit > Find and replace, or press ⌘F to search. The official page describes two options, Match case and Match using regular expressions.

Say your glossary says the client uses 'Partner' and not 'Associate'. Search for 'Associate' in the translated copy. Press Return to move to the next match. Fix each hit, then keep going until the search runs out of matches.

Turn on Match case when capitals change meaning, such as a brand name. Leave it off for common words. Turn on Match using regular expressions only when you need a pattern. A pattern can match far more text than you expect, so test it on a small copy first.

blocks.title: Find has blind spots
blocks.text: The official find page does not mention comments, footnotes, headers or footers. Do not assume a term check covered them. Run the short test below before you rely on Find.
How do you test whether Find reaches comments and footnotes?
A short test saves a bad hand-off. Run it on a copy so the real file stays clean.

items: Make a copy of the file with File > Make a copy.
Add one unique word, such as zqtest, in a comment, in a footnote and in the header.
Press ⌘F, search for that word, and check which places show up.
Note which places Find reaches and which it misses.
Delete the copy when you finish.

blocks.text: If Find misses a place, search that place by hand. Write the result in your notes, so you do not repeat the test from scratch next time.
Does offline editing work for Google Docs on a Mac?

Yes, in Chrome or Edge. Google's offline help page says offline editing requires Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge and the Google Docs Offline Chrome extension. Private browsing does not work. Offline access is a browser feature, so Safari and Firefox are not on that list.
Turn it on from Drive Settings. You can also open See document status and choose Turn on. The help page covers both paths. It does not give Mac steps.

The limits matter when you travel. Only the most recently opened documents save to your computer. Only one account per browser profile can have offline access. An administrator can turn it off. Very large files can fail to sync, and Google suggests splitting them.

items: Open the files you need before you leave, so they count as recently opened.
Use one Google account per browser profile if you need offline access.
Ask your administrator if the setting is missing, since an admin can disable it.
Split very large files into parts before you travel.

blocks.text: The offline help page says offline access turns on by itself if Drive for desktop is installed. It gives no more detail. Install Drive for desktop, check the setting, then test it with Wi-Fi off.

blocks.title: Safari users
blocks.text: Open the file in Chrome for offline work. The official offline page names only Chrome and Microsoft Edge as the browsers it requires.
Mistakes translators make in Google Docs on Mac
These mistakes cost the most time. Most of them come from assuming a menu does more than it does.

items: Editing the original file instead of the translated copy. Work in the copy and keep the source unchanged.
Assuming translation covers comments and footnotes. Check them by hand every time.
Trusting Find to search every part of the file. Run the short test first.
Working offline in Safari, where the official page does not list support.
Ignoring file size. Very large files can fail to sync, so split them into parts.
Accepting dictated terms without a read. Check each term against your glossary.

blocks.text: Each mistake has the same fix. Read the output as a draft, test each tool before you trust it, and check the parts the help page leaves out.
Is Google Docs enough for professional translation work?

Google Docs handles document-level work well. It covers a first pass, term checks, review, and client files that arrive as Google files. Google's translation help pages do not describe translation memory, termbases or segment-level tools.

Many translators do use dedicated tools. A 2024 survey of 96 ATA Law Division members found that 28.13% do not use CAT tools. SDL Trados was used by 43.75%. That survey asked about CAT tools, not Google Docs, and it covers one division only.

A ProZ survey of over 3,000 full-time professional translators reports that 88% use at least one CAT tool for some tasks. The article gives no survey year and does not mention Google Docs. Read it as a sign of CAT use in general, not of Docs use.
For a full CAT workflow, read [Word for translators on Mac](/for/translators/word). Use Google Docs for drafts, reviews and files that already live in Drive.
Where Lazur helps in Google Docs
Lazur is a voice assistant for the Mac. It lives in the notch. Hold ⌥ ⌘ to ask about anything on screen, and Lazur answers out loud. It looks at your screen only while you hold the shortcut.

Ask where something is, and Lazur draws a circle and a label around it. Ask how to do something, and Lazur guides you one click at a time, waiting for each click. Lazur does not click buttons or edit files for you.

Hold fn to dictate clean, formatted text at the cursor in any app. Add your glossary terms to the personal dictionary. Keep frequent phrases as snippets, and use clipboard slots for terms you paste often.

Audio and the screenshot go to AI providers to answer you. They are not stored, and content is never used to train AI models. For the Docs side of Lazur, see the [AI assistant for Google Docs on Mac](/apps/google-docs) page.
Worked example: one translation pass in Google Docs
Here is one full pass on a client file, from start to finish. The order matters.

items: Convert the file to Google Docs if Translate document is missing.
Run Tools > Translate document, and keep the new copy in Drive.
Open Edit > Find and replace and check each glossary term in the copy.
Check comments, footnotes, headers and footers by hand.
Turn on offline access in Chrome if you will work away from a connection.
Tell the client which parts you checked by hand, and which you did not.

blocks.text: Notice the order. Translation comes first, term checks second, and the manual check last. If you check terms before the translation, you check text that will change. If you skip the manual check, the gaps go to the client.
Dictation for translator notes on Mac
Hold fn, speak, and let go. Dictation writes clean text at the cursor, in Google Docs or any other app. Use it for translator notes, comments to the client and draft replies.

Do not dictate final translated text without a read. Speech input can get a term wrong, and a wrong term in a contract is costly. Read every term against your glossary before the file leaves your Mac.
Next steps for translators on a Mac

items: Run Translate document on a copy of a short file, and read the result.
Test Find with one word in a comment, a footnote and a header.
Turn on offline access in Chrome, then test it with Wi-Fi off.
Build a glossary list, and add the terms to your personal dictionary.

faq.question: Is there a separate Google Docs app for translators on Mac?
faq.answer: Google's help pages describe Google Docs in a browser. They do not describe a separate Mac app. Use Chrome or another browser on your Mac, and use Chrome or Edge if you need offline editing.

faq.question: Where is Translate document in Google Docs on Mac?
faq.answer: Open the file, click Tools in the menu bar, then choose Translate document. If the command is missing, the file is likely in Microsoft Office editing mode. Convert it to Google Docs first.

faq.question: Does Google Docs translate comments and footnotes?
faq.answer: The official translate page does not say which parts of a document get translated. It does not name comments or footnotes. Check both by hand in the translated copy.

faq.question: Does Find and replace search comments, footnotes and headers?
faq.answer: The official find page does not mention comments, footnotes, headers or footers. Test it on a copy. Put one unique word in each place, then search for that word.

faq.question: Can I use Google Docs offline in Safari on Mac?
faq.answer: The official offline page says offline editing requires Google Chrome or Microsoft Edge. Use Chrome for offline work. Private browsing does not work.

faq.question: How many documents can I keep available offline?
faq.answer: The offline help page says only the most recently opened documents save to your computer. Open the files you need before you travel, and check that they are available.

faq.question: Is Google Docs good enough for translation work?
faq.answer: It works well for a first pass, term checks and review. Its help pages do not describe translation memory or termbase tools. Use a CAT tool when a client needs those features.

faq.question: Can Lazur edit my Google Doc for me?
faq.answer: No. Lazur guides, points, explains, answers out loud, drafts and types text. It does not click buttons, edit files or operate other apps for you.

faq.question: Can dictation replace typing when I translate?
faq.answer: Dictation helps with notes, comments and draft replies. Hold fn to dictate clean text at the cursor. Read every term against your glossary before you send the file.
